title: Starship Flight 15: the first attempt to catch both stages
seoTitle: Starship Flight 15: launch time, countdown and what to watch
description: Starship Flight 15 targets Friday 13 November 2026 from Starbase Pad 2: live countdown, the double-catch plan, why the heat shield matters, and where to watch.
ogImageAlt: Starship Flight 15 title card on a dark background with the Supercharged Daily bolt
summary: SpaceX is targeting Starship Flight 15 for Friday 13 November 2026 from Pad 2 at Starbase, pending regulatory approval. The 75-minute window opens at 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC). That is a published window, not a guaranteed lift-off time.

For the first time SpaceX plans to try to catch both stages with the tower: Super Heavy minutes after launch, and the Ship after a flight of more than 22 hours. SpaceX's flight plan has the Ship deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites and make roughly 14 orbits before its deorbit burn; reports put the orbit at about 275 km.

If both catches work, it would be the first full recovery of an orbital launch system. The tower has caught a Super Heavy booster three times, on Flights 5, 7 and 8 (October 2024 to March 2025); it has never caught a Ship.
Alex R's 12 November minute-by-minute video — countdown to Saturday's Ship catch, using SpaceX's published times — is on the Ship 42 page and as a direct link under Where to watch.

heatShield.lead: Bringing the Ship home intact means surviving re-entry, and that is the heat shield's job.

points.text: Thousands of small hexagonal tiles cover the Ship's windward side. Because the Ship is mostly a plain cylinder, most tiles can share one shape and the rest are machined to fit, CNBC reported in August 2021.
In a 2019 test SpaceX heated tiles to about 1,650 K (around 1,377 °C or 2,510 °F), its estimate of orbital re-entry temperature, Digital Trends reported.
Most tiles are attached mechanically rather than glued, and SpaceX makes them in-house, according to Air & Space (December 2021). The space shuttle's glued tiles needed long repairs between flights.

updates.text: Ship 42 is in orbit and the Ship catch is still planned for Saturday. CBS News reports a single Raptor relit for about 10 seconds to put the Ship into its planned orbit, and that a deorbit burn is expected at 3:21 p.m. EST on Saturday (20:21 UTC) ahead of a catch attempt at the pad. We have not seen confirmation that the 26 Starlink V3 satellites were deployed.

No booster catch. Gizmodo reports SpaceX opted not to catch Super Heavy and diverted it to a splashdown in the Gulf, and that SpaceX does not yet know the cause. CBS News says controllers diverted the booster because of a technical problem. The time on this entry is approximate.
Lift-off. Starship Flight 15 launched from Starbase at 5:47 p.m. ET (22:47 UTC), per Gizmodo and CBS News.

Tesla Oracle reports the FAA has granted the Flight 15 licence, a little more than three hours before the window, citing a post by Sawyer Merritt on X. We have not seen an FAA or SpaceX statement ourselves. At our 21:50 UTC check we found no report of a changed launch time: the window is still listed as opening at 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC).

Alex R posted a minute-by-minute Flight 15 animation on X, using SpaceX's published timeline. If the window opens on time, the Ship catch is Saturday afternoon, about 22 and a half hours after Friday lift-off. Times are local Starbase (CST) and move if the launch slips.

Re-checked SpaceX's Flight 15 mission page on 13 Nov 2026: still as soon as Friday 13 November from Pad 2, 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC), 75-minute window, pending regulatory approval. Dual catch, 26 Starlink V3, more than 22 hours, webcast about 30 minutes before liftoff. This is a re-check, not a new date.

SpaceX: Ship 42 moved to the Starbase pad ahead of launch. The Flight 15 window is still as soon as Friday 13 November, 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC), 75 minutes, pending regulatory approval. Webcast about 30 minutes before liftoff. No FAA licence is published.
SpaceX lists Flight 15 as soon as Friday 13 November, 4:45 p.m. CT (22:45 UTC), 75-minute window, pending regulatory approval.

We checked this page against sources. The heat shield has thousands of tiles (CNBC), not a confirmed 18,000; the temperature is SpaceX's 2019 test figure (about 1,377 °C), not 1,400 °C; two unsourced claims (the gap-sealing felt and the tile factory's output) were removed; the booster-catch count (three) and the 14 orbits are now attributed.
